nodes.subject: Key rollover article
nodes.object: NKRO independently scans keys so simultaneous held keys can still be detected, a property relevant to multi-key gaming inputs.

support_spans.exact_quote: Key rollover is the ability of a computer keyboard to correctly handle several simultaneous keystrokes, often important in gaming as well as for testing rapid key pressing and reaction time. A keyboard with n -key rollover ( NKRO ) can correctly detect input from each key on the keyboard at the same time, regardless of how many other keys are also being pressed.

This means that each key is scanned completely independently by the keyboard hardware, so that each keypress is correctly detected regardless of how many other keys are being pressed or held down at the time.

nodes.subject: Keyboard technology article
nodes.object: Optical keyboards use light emitters and photo sensors without physical sensing contact, while keyboard processors debounce oscillating contacts to confirm one keystroke.

support_spans.exact_quote: An optical keyboard technology utilizes light-emitting devices and photo sensors to optically detect actuated keys, offering faster response times and eliminating the need for physical contact between moving parts.
To resolve this, the processor in a keyboard debounces the keystrokes, by averaging the signal over time to produce one "confirmed" keystroke that (usually) corresponds to a single press or release.

nodes.subject: mechanical-versus-optical thread participants
nodes.object: Participants describe fewer optical switch options and possible debounce-related latency benefits while explicitly lacking evidence that the difference is noticeable.

support_spans.exact_quote: The reason I know is that there are very few options for optical switches rn while for mechanical switches, it's endless.

They have less latency (I don't know too much, but apparently using optical switches can offer lower latency than mechanical switches because they have to work around something called debounce. So while it technically can reduce latency, I haven't seen anything regarding the difference in latency and whether it's an amount that someone would or could even notice in the context of everything else that adds latency.)

nodes.subject: Polling article
nodes.object: Polling actively samples external-device status, and a polling cycle trades response speed against processor or bandwidth overhead.

support_spans.exact_quote: Polling , or interrogation , refers to actively sampling the status of an external device by a client program as a synchronous activity.

A polling cycle is the time in which each element is monitored once. The optimal polling cycle will vary according to several factors, including the desired speed of response and the overhead (e.g., processor time and bandwidth ) of the polling.

nodes.subject: Hertz article
nodes.object: Hertz is one periodic event per second.

support_spans.exact_quote: The hertz is defined as one per second for periodic events.
One hertz (i.e. one per second) simply means "one periodic event occurs per second"

nodes.subject: USB HID article
nodes.object: A USB HID host periodically polls the interrupt endpoint and devices such as keyboards send reports in reply.

support_spans.exact_quote: The host periodically polls the device's interrupt IN endpoint during operation. When the device has data to send it forms a report and sends it as a reply to the poll token. Common devices such as keyboards and mice send reports that are compliant with standards set by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF).

nodes.subject: N-key rollover
nodes.object: NKRO means each key can be detected independently while other keys are held, preventing missed or ghosted multi-key combinations. This is physically useful for some gaming inputs, but the definition does not establish faster single-key actuation, lower end-to-end latency, or improved aim.

accepted_phrases: NKRO independently detects simultaneous keys and addresses multi-key loss, ghosting, and jamming; that rollover property is not itself evidence of lower single-key latency or better aim.

support_spans.exact_quote: Key rollover is the ability of a computer keyboard to correctly handle several simultaneous keystrokes, often important in gaming as well as for testing rapid key pressing and reaction time. A keyboard with n -key rollover ( NKRO ) can correctly detect input from each key on the keyboard at the same time, regardless of how many other keys are also being pressed.

This means that each key is scanned completely independently by the keyboard hardware, so that each keypress is correctly detected regardless of how many other keys are being pressed or held down at the time.
Some computer games require multiple keys (other than the usual modifier keys) to be held down while others are pressed and released, in order to perform actions simultaneously

nodes.subject: optical sensing and keyboard debouncing
nodes.object: Optical keyboards use emitters and photo sensors, can offer faster response, and avoid physical contact between moving sensing parts. Debouncing addresses contact oscillation that could register multiple keystrokes. These generic mechanisms do not measure the SK61 or K6 end-to-end latency or human perceptibility.

accepted_phrases: Optical sensing and contact debouncing are physically real mechanisms, but their generic descriptions do not measure either frozen keyboard's total latency or prove a perceptible gaming benefit.

support_spans.exact_quote: An optical keyboard technology utilizes light-emitting devices and photo sensors to optically detect actuated keys, offering faster response times and eliminating the need for physical contact between moving parts.
When a key is pressed, it oscillates ( bounces ) against its contacts several times before settling. When released, it oscillates again until it comes to rest.
To resolve this, the processor in a keyboard debounces the keystrokes, by averaging the signal over time to produce one "confirmed" keystroke that (usually) corresponds to a single press or release.

nodes.subject: mechanical-versus-optical community discussion
nodes.object: Thread participants describe a smaller optical-switch ecosystem, possible response or debounce-related latency advantages, and explicit uncertainty about whether the latency difference is noticeable. These are scoped opinions, not instrumented SK61-versus-K6 results.

accepted_phrases: Community participants describe optical-switch choice limits and possible latency advantages while explicitly saying they have not seen evidence that the difference is noticeable; the thread is not an instrumented comparison of the SK61 and K6.

support_spans.exact_quote: The reason I know is that there are very few options for optical switches rn while for mechanical switches, it's endless.

They actuate faster (Sometimes, but not always as this just depends on the actuation distance. Some mechanical switches, often called speed switches, offer shorter actuation points, but it isn't always desired since it can also increase the frequency of fat finger mistakes)

They have less latency (I don't know too much, but apparently using optical switches can offer lower latency than mechanical switches because they have to work around something called debounce. So while it technically can reduce latency, I haven't seen anything regarding the difference in latency and whether it's an amount that someone would or could even notice in the context of everything else that adds latency.)

nodes.subject: computer polling
nodes.object: Polling actively samples an external device, and a polling cycle is the time to monitor each element once. The desired response speed and processing or bandwidth overhead affect the appropriate cycle; this generic definition does not specify either keyboard's polling rate.

accepted_phrases: Polling is repeated status sampling with a cycle-time and overhead tradeoff; the generic definition does not establish a polling rate for either frozen keyboard.

nodes.subject: hypothetical polling frequency
nodes.object: Hertz means events per second. If a device actually polls at 8000 Hz, one poll period is 0.125 ms; at 1000 Hz it is 1 ms. The 0.875 ms period difference is arithmetic only and does not equal a measured end-to-end latency or perception threshold.

accepted_phrases: Because hertz means events per second, hypothetical 8000 Hz and 1000 Hz poll periods are 0.125 ms and 1 ms; their 0.875 ms difference is not by itself an end-to-end latency or perceptibility result.

support_spans.exact_quote: The hertz is defined as one per second for periodic events.
One hertz (i.e. one per second) simply means "one periodic event occurs per second"

nodes.subject: USB HID report transfer
nodes.object: During USB HID operation the host periodically polls the device interrupt endpoint, and keyboards can send reports in reply. This connects polling to keyboard reports but provides no rate or end-to-end measurement for the two products.

accepted_phrases: USB HID hosts periodically poll an interrupt endpoint and keyboards return reports, but the generic protocol description supplies no polling rate or full latency for either candidate.

When the device has data to send it forms a report and sends it as a reply to the poll token. Common devices such as keyboards and mice send reports that are compliant with standards set by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF).

nodes.subject: candidate NKRO claim scope
nodes.object: The seller pages claim NKRO and the concept page explains why simultaneous-key detection can matter in gaming. That evidence supports a real rollover feature but not a faster single key, lower end-to-end latency, or improved aim.

nodes.subject: optical mechanism and owner-claim scope
nodes.object: Optical sensing and contact debouncing are real mechanisms. The SK61 implements optical switches, while community participants describe both possible response advantages and a restricted switch ecosystem, yet explicitly lack evidence that the latency difference is noticeable. No captured source provides an instrumented SK61-versus-K6 latency or aim test.

nodes.subject: 8000 Hz polling claim boundary
nodes.object: USB HID polling is a real report path and hertz permits a hypothetical 0.125 ms period at 8000 Hz versus 1 ms at 1000 Hz. Because neither product body states an actual polling rate and no source measures the rest of the input-to-display path or human perception, the arithmetic cannot justify an 8000 Hz premium here.
